title: Training novices to think, or giving them LLMs? Evidence from an RCT
pdf_filename: Asirvatham et al (2026) - Training Novices to Think or Giving Them LLMs.pdf
review_note: Codex checked Tables A.7-A.11 and the experimental procedures against the downloaded PDF. No human research assistant has verified this addition.

paper_metadata.authors_full: Hemanth Asirvatham, Chiara Betti, Rachel Brown, Arnaldo Camuffo, Aaron Chatterji, Chiara Fumagalli, Alfonso Gambardella, Myriam Mariani, Abhinav Pandey, Steve Ramos, Giovanni Salvucci, Vladimir Simic
paper_metadata.incentives: Conducted during regular class hours; no participant payment or performance incentive is reported
paper_metadata.summary: Classroom experiment with 1,053 first-year undergraduates, crossing causal-reasoning training with ChatGPT Edu access. ChatGPT improved the rated quality of business recommendations and coherent reasoning in the submitted work. Students could use AI during the assessment; the study did not test subsequent performance without AI.
paper_metadata.pdf_filename: Asirvatham et al (2026) - Training Novices to Think or Giving Them LLMs.pdf

summary.setup: In November 2025, 1,053 first-year students in 13 introductory management classes at a European university took part over two consecutive days. Classes were assigned within three degree programs to a causal-reasoning training game or a placebo game, crossed with ChatGPT Edu access or no AI access. Students then wrote a business recommendation about university merchandise. ChatGPT Edu used GPT-4o and remained available to the AI groups while they wrote. The main text withholds the university's name; appendix materials refer to Bocconi. There was no subsequent assessment without AI. Several authors were employed by OpenAI or contributed as paid contractors.
summary.empirical_strategy: The four conditions contained 249 control students, 256 with causal training only, 197 with AI only, and 351 with both. The allocation description implies three classes in each of the first three conditions and four in the combined condition. OLS regressions include the training indicator, AI indicator, their interaction, and baseline balance controls. The AI coefficient compares AI-only with control. Adding the AI and interaction coefficients gives the AI effect among trained students. All regressions use 1,053 students. Reported standard errors use groups formed from class, mother tongue, and high-school type, which subdivide the 13 randomized classes. The atlas omits confidence intervals and pooled weights because class-level standard errors are unavailable. Standardized point estimates use the full-sample outcome SDs in Table A.7.
summary.key_results: Without causal training, AI access raised the rated recommendation score by 0.862 points on the 1-to-5 scale and coherent logic by 0.214 points. The estimated changes in mechanism identification and falsifiability were -0.008 and 0.029 points. With causal training, the corresponding AI effects were 0.944, 0.442, 0.121, and 0.232 points, calculated by adding the AI and interaction coefficients. The site also records similarity to three expert recommendations. These outcomes describe work produced with AI available. They do not establish that students acquired or retained the skills. The reported precision does not account for assignment at the class level, so the atlas does not attach significance claims to these estimates.

sample.source_locator: Appendix Section 1, printed p. 16 (PDF p. 17); Table A.8, printed p. 42 (PDF p. 43). Class counts are derived from one class per program per condition, with one extra Management class in Causal&GPT.

extraction_rules.specification: Use the balance-controlled regressions plotted in the main text: Table A.9 columns 1-3, Table A.10 column 2, and Table A.11 columns 2, 4, and 6. Unadjusted alternatives are retained below for source comparison.
extraction_rules.contrasts: GPT versus Control, and Causal&GPT versus Causal. Both isolate AI access holding the training condition fixed. The interaction coefficient alone is not the second contrast. Training-only effects and game outcomes measured before AI access are not effects of AI.
extraction_rules.standardization: Divide the coefficient by its full-sample outcome SD from Table A.7. These are post-treatment full-sample SD units, not control-arm SDs. Calculations are in code/audit/asirvatham_learning.do.
extraction_rules.precision: Keep the reported coefficients, SEs, and significance thresholds here. Leave website se, ci_lower, and ci_upper null. Reported groups subdivide randomized classes; the covariance needed for conditional AI-effect SEs is also unavailable. Do not reconstruct precision from sample size or significance stars.
extraction_rules.scope: Seven task-performance and reasoning outcomes enter the learning section as measured with AI. Table A.12 idea count and diversity belong to the separate creativity extraction and are not added to the learning collection. Post-treatment-adjusted mediation regressions are not total treatment effects.

estimates.treatment: Causal-reasoning training and ChatGPT Edu access during the business task
estimates.control: Causal-reasoning training and no AI access during the business task
estimates.notes: Table A.11, column (6), printed p. 44 (PDF p. 45), balance-controlled OLS. Causal&GPT versus Causal. AI effect among trained students = GPT coefficient (0.044) + interaction (-0.002) = 0.042 cosine similarity. The interaction alone is not this effect. Its standard error cannot be recovered without the coefficient covariance. Standardized point estimate = 0.042 / 0.050, using the full-sample post-treatment SD in Table A.7, printed p. 41 (PDF p. 42). This is not a control-arm SD. Standard errors clustered at the randomized-class level are unavailable. The paper clusters by class, mother tongue, and high-school type, creating groups within the randomized classes. The atlas therefore omits confidence intervals and pooled weights. N=1,053 is the estimation sample across all four conditions. The treatment and control counts describe the two conditions in this contrast and do not sum to the regression N. Assignment occurred across 13 classes. Counts come from Table A.8 and Appendix Section 1. An embedding-based cosine similarity compares each recommendation with the named expert reference. This is a proxy for alignment with the reference, not an independently administered knowledge test. AI was available during the assessment. No subsequent unaided test was administered.
